prompt: In atomic spectra, what does the term fine structure mean?

choices.text: A line is really a set of closely spaced lines
A line is much weaker than the lines near it
choices.why: Fine structure is about spacing, not intensity: one line turns out to be a multiplet of lines spaced close together.

choices.text: A line lies far outside the visible region
choices.why: Fine structure has nothing to do with where a line lies. "Fine" means finely spaced: a line splits into closely spaced lines.

choices.text: A line appears in absorption but not in emission
choices.why: Fine structure shows up in both. The term means that a line is a multiplet, two or more lines spaced close together.

explanation: At high resolution many lines turn out to be multiplets: two or more closely spaced lines (two make a doublet, three a triplet). Multiplets are also called fine structure, because the lines are finely spaced.

prompt: The Hα line of hydrogen comes from an electron going from n = 3 to n = 2, yet at high resolution it is a doublet. What did this fine structure reveal?

choices.text: An orbital energy-level diagram is incomplete
The Hα line does not come from n = 3 → n = 2
choices.why: The Hα line is still a 3 → 2 transition. The doublet shows that each n holds several levels that an orbital diagram doesn't show.

choices.text: Hydrogen's energy does not depend on n at all
choices.why: n still sets the coarse energy. Fine structure adds small splittings on top of it, which the orbital picture leaves out.

choices.text: A hydrogen atom has two electrons, not one
choices.why: Hydrogen has one electron. The doublet comes from that electron's spin interacting with its orbital motion, which an orbital diagram ignores.

explanation: The observation of fine structure showed that an orbital energy-level diagram does not completely describe the energy levels of atoms. Levels with the same n can have slightly different energies.

prompt: At the time it was found, the fine structure of hydrogen's spectral lines gave key evidence for what?

choices.text: The existence of electron spin
The existence of the atomic nucleus
choices.why: The nucleus was known from other experiments. Fine structure pointed to electron spin, which explains the multiplets and their splittings.

choices.text: The wave nature of light
choices.why: Fine structure tells us about the atom's energy levels, not about light. It gave key evidence for electron spin.

choices.text: The existence of the neutron
choices.why: Neutrons don't split hydrogen's lines. The multiplets were explained by electron spin, which also gave highly accurate splittings.

explanation: Electron spin gave a qualitative explanation for the multiplets, and it also allowed highly accurate calculations of the multiplet splittings. So fine structure was key evidence for spin.

prompt: Why does the configuration 2p^1 not, on its own, pin down the electronic state of a hydrogen atom?

choices.text: Its orbital, spin and total angular momenta aren't fixed
It doesn't tell us which shell n the electron occupies
choices.why: The 2 in 2p^1 gives n = 2. What's missing is which orbital and spin the electron has, and how its angular momenta combine.

choices.text: A p electron has no angular momentum that needs specifying
choices.why: A p electron has l = 1, and it also has spin. Those momenta can combine in more than one way, which the configuration doesn't say.

choices.text: Its energy depends mainly on the spin of the nucleus
choices.why: The section doesn't involve the nucleus's spin. The problem is that the electron's orbital, spin and total angular momenta are not specified.

explanation: In 2p^1 the electron can be in any of the three p orbitals with either spin, and its orbital and spin angular momenta can combine in more than one way. These combinations can have different energies, so the configuration alone doesn't identify the state.

prompt: Why do an electron's spin and its orbital motion interact with each other?

choices.text: Both produce magnetic dipole moments
Both produce electric dipole moments
choices.why: The interaction is magnetic. The orbital motion and the spin each produce a magnetic dipole, and the two dipoles interact like tiny bar magnets.

choices.text: The spin is what drives the orbital motion
choices.why: Spin and orbital motion are separate sources of angular momentum. They interact because each one produces a magnetic dipole moment.

choices.text: Both are pulled together by the nucleus
choices.why: The nucleus's attraction holds the electron in the atom; it isn't what couples spin and orbit. The coupling comes from their magnetic dipole moments.

explanation: Both the electron's spin and its orbital motion produce magnetic dipole moments. These dipoles interact like two tiny bar magnets attracting and repelling each other; this is the spin–orbit interaction.

prompt: The spin–orbit interaction energy is written E_(s-o) ∝ S·L. What does this say?

choices.text: It goes as the dot product of S and L
It goes as the vector sum S + L
choices.why: S + L is the total angular momentum J. The energy goes as the scalar (dot) product S·L, because it comes from two interacting magnetic dipoles.

choices.text: It depends only on the size of the spin S
choices.why: S·L involves both the spin and the orbital angular momentum, and how they are oriented to each other, not the spin alone.

choices.text: It is the same for every way S and L combine
choices.why: The scalar product depends on how S and L are oriented, so different combinations have different energies. That is what splits the lines.

explanation: The interaction energy is proportional to the scalar product of the two magnetic dipole moments, which are proportional to the angular momentum vectors, so E_(s-o) ∝ S·L. The constant of proportionality is called the spin–orbit coupling constant.

prompt: The section compares describing coupled spin and orbital motion separately to describing two coupled bar magnets independently. What is the point of the comparison?

choices.text: Coupled motions must be described together
An electron is really a tiny bar magnet
choices.why: The bar magnets are an analogy for the coupling. The point is that once spin and orbit interact, they can't be described separately.

choices.text: Spin and orbital motion never affect each other
choices.why: The comparison says the opposite: like two coupled magnets, spin and orbit interact, so they can't be described independently.

choices.text: The magnets cancel, so the coupling energy is zero
choices.why: Coupled magnets attract and repel, so there is an interaction energy. The point is that the interaction must be taken into account.

explanation: Because of spin–orbit coupling, exact wavefunctions are not eigenfunctions of the spin and orbital angular momentum operators separately. As with two coupled bar magnets, the interaction must be included, and the total angular momentum J = L + S is used.

prompt: In the hydrogen 2p^1 configuration, the electron can be in any of the three p orbitals (m_l = +1, 0, −1), with m_s = +1/2 or −1/2. How many different states does this give?
explanation: 3 orbitals × 2 spins = 6 states. Table 8.11.1 agrees: the ^2P_(1/2) level has 2 states and ^2P_(3/2) has 4, which add up to 6.

prompt: For one electron moving from one atomic orbital to another by absorbing or emitting light, what is the selection rule on l?

choices.text: Δl = ±1
Δl = 0
choices.why: l must change. A photon has spin 1, so the electron's orbital angular momentum changes by one unit: Δl = ±1.
That form, with 0 allowed, is the Russell–Saunders rule for the total L. For a single electron, Δl = ±1.

choices.text: Δl = ±2
choices.why: A change of two units is forbidden. The photon carries one unit of angular momentum, so Δl = ±1.

explanation: The selection rules for a single electron are Δl = ±1 and Δm_l = 0, ±1. For example, 2p → 1s is allowed, but 2s → 1s (Δl = 0) and 3d → 1s (Δl = −2) are not.

prompt: According to the section, where do the selection rules Δl = ±1 and Δm_l = 0, ±1 come from?

choices.text: Angular momentum is conserved; a photon has spin 1
Energy is conserved; a photon has no spin
choices.why: A photon does carry angular momentum: it has spin 1. Conservation of angular momentum is what makes l change by one unit.

choices.text: An electron's charge cannot change in a transition
choices.why: Charge is conserved, but that doesn't restrict l. The rules come from conservation of angular momentum and the photon's spin of 1.

choices.text: Only orbitals of the same energy can be connected
choices.why: A transition joins levels of different energy; the photon carries the difference. The rule on l comes from angular momentum conservation.

explanation: The selection rules arise from the conservation of angular momentum during a spectroscopic transition and the fact that a photon has spin 1. The photon brings in or carries away angular momentum, so the electron's l must change.

prompt: An electron in hydrogen drops from an n = 3 orbital (3s, 3p or 3d) to an n = 2 orbital (2s or 2p), which gives six possible pairs. Using the selection rule Δl = ±1, how many of the six are allowed?
explanation: Allowed: 3s → 2p (Δl = +1), 3p → 2s (Δl = −1) and 3d → 2p (Δl = −1). Forbidden: 3s → 2s and 3p → 2p (Δl = 0), and 3d → 2s (Δl = −2). So 3 are allowed.

prompt: Which of these transitions is allowed by the Russell–Saunders selection rules ΔS = 0, ΔL = 0, ±1 and ΔJ = 0, ±1?

choices.why: Here L goes from 2 to 0 (ΔL = −2) and J from 5/2 to 1/2 (ΔJ = −2). Both are outside the rules.
This goes from a triplet (S = 1) to a singlet (S = 0), so ΔS ≠ 0. In L–S coupling it is forbidden.
ΔL = −1 is fine, but J goes from 5/2 to 1/2, so ΔJ = −2, which is forbidden.

explanation: For ^2P_(3/2) → ^2S_(1/2), S stays 1/2 (ΔS = 0), L goes from 1 to 0 (ΔL = −1) and J from 3/2 to 1/2 (ΔJ = −1). All the rules are met. Sodium's D lines are transitions of this kind.

prompt: What does the Russell–Saunders selection rule ΔS = 0 require of a transition?

choices.text: The total spin S stays the same
The electron's spin must flip
choices.why: A spin flip would change S. The rule says the total spin can't change: singlets go to singlets, doublets to doublets.

choices.text: S must change by one, like l
choices.why: It is the jumping electron's l that changes by one. The total spin S must stay the same.

choices.text: Only atoms with S = 0 can absorb light
choices.why: Atoms with any S can absorb light; sodium has S = 1/2. The rule only says that S must be the same before and after.

explanation: ΔS = 0 means the spin multiplicity can't change in a transition (within L–S coupling): a singlet goes to a singlet and a triplet to a triplet. A singlet-to-triplet transition is forbidden.

prompt: The rule for one electron is Δl = ±1, yet the Russell–Saunders rules allow ΔL = 0. Why is there no contradiction?

choices.text: The electron's l changes; the total L need not
ΔL = 0 lines break angular momentum conservation
choices.why: The section says ΔL = 0 does not violate conservation of angular momentum, because Δl = ±1 is still required of the electron.

choices.text: L and l are the same, so ΔL = 0 means Δl = 0
choices.why: l belongs to one electron; L is the total orbital angular momentum of the state. They are different quantum numbers.

choices.text: In a ΔL = 0 transition the photon has no spin
choices.why: A photon always has spin 1. The electron's l changes by one unit; it's the overall L of the state that can stay the same.

explanation: The orbital angular momentum of the electron that jumps must change (Δl = ±1). But the total L of the state, which combines all the electrons, doesn't have to change, so ΔL = 0 is allowed.

prompt: The Russell–Saunders rule ΔJ = 0, ±1 allows ΔJ = 0. Which transition with ΔJ = 0 is still forbidden?

choices.text: From a J = 0 level to a J = 0 level
From a J = 1/2 level to a J = 1/2 level
choices.why: This is allowed; sodium's ^2P_(1/2) → ^2S_(1/2) line is one. Only J = 0 to J = 0 is excluded.

choices.text: From a J = 1 level to a J = 1 level
choices.why: ΔJ = 0 between two J = 1 levels is allowed. The only exception is J = 0 to J = 0.

choices.text: From a J = 2 level to a J = 2 level
choices.why: This is allowed by ΔJ = 0. Only the transition from J = 0 to J = 0 is forbidden.

explanation: ΔJ can be 0, +1 or −1, with one exception: a transition from J = 0 to J = 0 is forbidden.

prompt: The rule ΔS = 0 forbids transitions between singlet (S = 0) and triplet (S = 1) states. Where are such transitions actually observed?

choices.text: In heavy atoms, where L–S coupling fails
In hydrogen and one-electron ions
choices.why: One electron always gives S = 1/2, so there are no singlets or triplets. Singlet–triplet lines appear in heavy atoms.

choices.text: In light atoms such as helium
choices.why: Light atoms are described well by L–S coupling, so ΔS = 0 holds. The rule breaks down as the atomic number increases.

choices.text: Nowhere; they are forbidden in every atom
choices.why: They are allowed and observed in heavy atoms. The Russell–Saunders rules apply only where L–S coupling describes the atom.

explanation: The Russell–Saunders rules apply only to atoms described by L–S coupling. As the atomic number increases, S and L become "bad" quantum numbers and jj coupling is more applicable, so singlet–triplet transitions are allowed and observed in heavy atoms.

prompt: Sodium vapor in the Sun's upper layers absorbs light near 589.5 nm, making a dark D line. Which change of sodium's valence electron absorbs this light?

choices.text: 3s → 3p
3p → 3d
choices.why: In the ground state sodium's valence electron is in 3s, not 3p. The D line is the 3s → 3p transition.

choices.text: 3s → 4s
choices.why: That has Δl = 0, which the rule Δl = ±1 forbids. The D line is 3s → 3p.

choices.text: 2p → 3s
choices.why: A 2p electron is an inner [Ne] electron, not the valence electron. The D line comes from the valence electron going 3s → 3p.

explanation: The D line corresponds to sodium's valence electron moving between the 3s and 3p states. In absorption it goes 3s → 3p; in emission, as in the yellow flame-test light, it goes 3p → 3s.

prompt: At high resolution, the sodium D line is two lines, D1 and D2. What causes the splitting?

choices.text: Spin–orbit coupling in the excited 3p state
Spin–orbit splitting of the 3s ground state
choices.why: A 3s electron has L = 0, so that state has only one level, ^2S_(1/2). The splitting is in the 3p state, which has L = 1.

choices.text: Two isotopes of sodium in the vapor
choices.why: No second isotope is needed: one sodium atom has two 3p levels, split apart by spin–orbit coupling.

choices.text: Repulsion between two 3p electrons
choices.why: Sodium has just one valence electron, with S = 1/2. The two lines come from spin–orbit coupling of that electron in the 3p state.

explanation: Na has one unpaired electron (S = 1/2). In the excited P state L = 1, so spin–orbit coupling gives two levels, with J = 3/2 and J = 1/2. Transitions between these two levels and the single ground level give the D1 and D2 lines.

prompt: Sodium's excited [Ne]3p^1 configuration has two levels. Which are they?

choices.why: One unpaired electron gives S = 1/2 and 2S + 1 = 2, so both levels are doublets, not a singlet and a triplet.
With S = 1/2 and L = 1, J is 3/2 or 1/2. J can't be a whole number when there is one unpaired electron.
^2S_(1/2) is the level of the 3s ground configuration. A p electron has L = 1, so both 3p levels are P levels.

explanation: One 3p electron gives S = 1/2 and L = 1, so J = 3/2 or 1/2. The two levels are ^2P_(3/2) and ^2P_(1/2), and transitions between them and ^2S_(1/2) give the two D lines.

prompt: The sodium D1 line is at 589.6 nm and the D2 line at 589.0 nm. Which line comes from photons of higher energy?

choices.text: D2, since its wavelength is shorter
D1, since its wavelength is longer
choices.why: Photon energy is E = hc/λ, so a longer wavelength means a lower energy. D2, at the shorter wavelength, has the higher energy.

choices.text: Neither; the two have the same energy
choices.why: Lines at different wavelengths have different photon energies, E = hc/λ. The difference here is small, about 0.1%, but real.

choices.text: It depends on the temperature of the flame
choices.why: The line positions are set by the atom's energy levels, not by the flame. With E = hc/λ, the shorter-wavelength D2 line has the higher energy.

explanation: Photon energy is E = hc/λ, so the shorter the wavelength, the higher the energy. D2 at 589.0 nm has slightly more energy than D1 at 589.6 nm.

prompt: Using E = hc/λ with hc = 1240 eV·nm, what is the energy of a photon in the sodium D2 line, at 589.0 nm, in eV?
explanation: E = (1240 eV·nm)/(589.0 nm) = 2.105 eV. This is the energy gap between one of the two 3p levels and the 3s ground level.

prompt: In Example 8.11.1, the 5S → 3P emission of sodium gives two lines, at 616.07 and 615.42 nm. Why two?

choices.text: The lower 3P state has two levels
The upper 5S state has two levels
choices.why: An S state has L = 0 and only one level, ^2S_(1/2). The two lines come from the two levels of the lower (terminal) 3P state.

choices.text: Sodium has two valence electrons
choices.why: Sodium, [Ne]3s^1, has one valence electron. The line splits because the 3P state it ends in has two levels.

choices.text: Each photon can have two spins
choices.why: The two lines have two different energies, set by the atom's levels. They come from the two levels of the terminal 3P state.

explanation: The 5S state has only one level, ^2S_(1/2), but the terminal 3P state has two, ^2P_(3/2) and ^2P_(1/2). The electron can end in either, so the transition gives two lines.

prompt: In Example 8.11.1, the 4D → 3P transition of sodium gives two lines, at 568.82 nm and 568.26 nm. How far apart are the two lines, in nm? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: 568.82 nm − 568.26 nm = 0.56 nm. The example explains the two lines by the two levels of the terminal 3P state.

prompt: There are n^2 orbitals with principal quantum number n, and an electron in any of them can have either of two spins. How many states are associated with n = 3 in hydrogen?
explanation: Number of states = 2 × n^2 = 2 × 3^2 = 2 × 9 = 18. Table 8.11.1 agrees: the n = 3 levels have degeneracies 2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 6 = 18.

prompt: The Hα line of hydrogen is at 656.279 nm, which is 6.56279 × 10^−5 cm. Using ν̃ = 1/λ, what is its wavenumber, in cm^−1?
explanation: ν̃ = 1/(6.56279 × 10^−5 cm) = 15,237 cm^−1. The doublet splitting of this line is only 0.326 cm^−1, about 2 parts in 100,000 of it, which is why high-resolution instruments were needed to see the fine structure.

prompt: With spin–orbit coupling and relativistic corrections, hydrogen levels with the same n and J have the same energy. Which pair of n = 3 levels has the same energy?

choices.why: These have different J values, so their energies differ; this is the spin–orbit splitting of the 3p term.
Different J values (3/2 and 5/2) give different energies, even though both levels come from 3d.
J is 1/2 for one and 5/2 for the other, so their energies differ.

explanation: Only n and J matter for the energy here. ^2P_(3/2) and ^2D_(3/2) both have n = 3 and J = 3/2, so they have the same energy, as do ^2S_(1/2) and ^2P_(1/2), both with J = 1/2.

prompt: The section says five transitions are allowed from hydrogen's n = 3 levels to its n = 2 levels. Why does the Hα line still appear as a doublet?

choices.text: Two are far more intense than the other three
Only two of the five obey the selection rules
choices.why: All five are allowed. Two of them are the most intense and make the doublet; the others add to the line widths or aren't observed.

choices.text: Three of them lie outside the visible region
choices.why: All five lie very close together, near 656 nm. The weaker three add to the width of the two lines or are not observed.

choices.text: The hydrogen and deuterium lines overlap
choices.why: The two isotopes give separate lines, Hα^1 and Hα^2. The doublet comes from the two most intense of the five transitions.

explanation: Of the five allowed transitions, two are the most intense and are responsible for the doublet. The other transitions contribute to the width of these lines or are not observed.

prompt: The theoretical splitting of hydrogen's Hα doublet is the difference between two term splittings, 0.364 cm^−1 and 0.036 cm^−1. What is the theoretical splitting, in cm^−1? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: 0.364 cm^−1 − 0.036 cm^−1 = 0.328 cm^−1. This is in excellent agreement with the measured splitting of 0.326 cm^−1.

prompt: Term symbols are needed to explain fine structure. Why are orbital configurations still useful for spectra?

choices.text: They explain a spectrum's coarse features
They give the exact energy of every level
choices.why: Configurations miss the splittings from spin–orbit coupling. They are useful for the coarse features and for picturing how electron density changes.

choices.text: They show how each line is split
choices.why: The splitting needs term symbols and their J values. Configurations give the coarse features of a spectrum.

choices.text: They make the selection rules unnecessary
choices.why: Selection rules still decide which transitions occur. Configurations help with coarse features and give a physical picture of the electron density.

explanation: Orbital configurations help us understand the general, or coarse, features of spectra, and they give a physical picture of how the electron density changes in a transition. Term symbols then explain the finer details.
